title: Intelligent Tutors Beyond K-12: An Observational Study of Adult Learner Engagement and Academic Impact
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether intelligent tutoring systems, which have mostly been studied in K-12 settings, can also benefit adult learners in postsecondary education when use is voluntary rather than required. The authors focus on two questions: how optional tutor use relates to adult learners’ academic outcomes, and what demographic or behavioral characteristics distinguish adults who choose to use intelligent tutors.

The intervention studied is the Apprentice Tutors platform, a set of adaptive College Algebra tutors integrated into Blackboard and Canvas via LTI at a state technical college. The tutors provided real-time correctness feedback, Bayesian Knowledge Tracing-based adaptive problem selection, multi-layered hints, progress tracking, tutorial videos, links to textbook and YouTube resources, and a bug/Q&A feature. The study analyzed two years of platform deployment data, combining tutor interaction logs with institutional grades and demographic records. Analyses included descriptive statistics, usage analyses, learning-curve modeling, and regression analysis.

The population was adult learners enrolled in College Algebra at a 2-year state technical college in the United States, many of whom balanced work with night, hybrid, in-person, or online study. The dataset included 3,510 students overall, with 520 students using the tutors at least once and 214 using them in Unit 1, which had the greatest tutor coverage. Tutor users were more likely to be female and slightly older than non-users, and usage was concentrated in evenings, late nights, and on Thursdays, suggesting that flexibility mattered for this learner population.

The main conclusion is that voluntary use of intelligent tutors appears promising for adult postsecondary learners. Students showed reduced error rates with more practice inside the tutors, and tutor use was positively associated with higher Unit 1 assessment scores outside the tutor. However, because the study was observational and lacked random assignment, the authors emphasize that these findings are preliminary and do not establish causality. They argue that intelligent tutors are a viable supplementary resource for adult learners and recommend future randomized studies and broader tutor coverage to test long-term and more generalizable effects.

identified_tools.name: Apprentice Tutors
identified_tools.description: A novel intelligent tutoring system platform for College Algebra that offers topic-specific tutors with adaptive problem selection using Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, real-time correctness feedback, multi-layer hints, progress tracking, and LMS integration via LTI.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as an optional supplemental tutoring resource for adult learners in a state technical college's College Algebra course, with analysis of voluntary usage, in-tutor learning, demographics, and associations with Unit 1 course assessment performance.

findings.finding_summary: Within the tutor, student error rates decreased with increasing practice opportunities, indicating skill improvement over time. The paper reports that students initially had an average error rate of approximately 65% per skill on their first attempt, and the decrease in predicted error rate over practice was significant (p < 0.001); the plotted learning curve included a 95% confidence interval, but no standardized effect size was reported.
findings.measure: Predicted error rate across skill practice opportunities in tutor log data modeled with pyAFM/Additive Factors Model
findings.confidence_interval: 95% confidence interval shown in Figure 8; exact interval not reported

findings.finding_summary: Tutor users achieved slightly higher mean grades on the Unit 1 assessment than non-tutor users, and the paper describes this as preliminary evidence that learning transferred outside the tutor. Because the study was observational, the authors explicitly state that causal inference cannot be made from this comparison; exact group means were not reported in the text, though Figure 9 shows 95% confidence intervals.
findings.measure: Unit 1 course assessment grades comparing tutor users vs. non-tutor users
findings.confidence_interval: 95% confidence intervals shown in Figure 9; exact interval not reported

findings.finding_summary: A linear regression found a significant positive relationship between amount of tutor use and Unit 1 grade. The Transactions predictor had estimate = 0.26, error = 0.08, t = 3.39, p < 0.001, with intercept = 66.57 (error = 0.34, t = 193.59, p < 0.001), suggesting more tutor transactions were associated with higher grades, though the authors note tutor usage explained only a small proportion of grade variance.
findings.measure: Linear regression of Unit 1 assessment grade on number of tutor transactions

quality_tier_rationale: This is an observational quasi-experimental study using platform logs, demographics, and course grades, but without randomization or a true control design. The authors explicitly note that causal conclusions cannot be drawn, so the evidence quality is correlational rather than experimental.
impact_tier_rationale: Findings are consistently positive but effect sizes are not standardized and the paper characterizes the grade relationship as modest, with tutor use accounting for only a small proportion of variance. Impact is therefore promising but unclear in magnitude.
